items.q: What are the four core OOP principles?
items.e: The 4 OOP principles: Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, Abstraction — the foundation of object-oriented programming.

o: Hiding an object's internal state and exposing access through methods
items.e: Encapsulation: private fields + public getters/setters. Protects the object's state from incorrect external changes.

o: One interface — different implementations; a method behaves differently depending on the object
A class has only one form
An object can be only one type
items.e: Polymorphism: one method — different behavior. Compile-time (overloading) and runtime (overriding through inheritance).

items.q: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
o: An abstract class can have state/constructor, a class extends only one; an interface — multiple implementation
An abstract class supports multiple inheritance, while an interface always has a single implementation
An abstract class can't have method implementations, while an interface always has a mandatory constructor
An interface stores object state and private fields, an abstract class is only used as a marker type
items.e: Abstract class: state, constructor, single inheritance. Interface: multiple implementation, since Java 8 — default/static methods.

o: A subclass provides its own implementation of a parent method with the same signature
A class defines several methods with the same name but different parameters
items.e: Overriding: the subclass redefines the parent's method with the same signature. The @Override annotation helps avoid mistakes.

o: Several methods with the same name but different parameters in one class
Redefining a method in a subclass
items.e: Overloading: methods with the same name but different parameter count/types. Resolved at compile time.

items.q: What does the final keyword do?
o: Class — can't be extended; method — can't be overridden; variable — a constant
items.e: final class (not extendable), final method (not overridable), final variable (assigned once).

o: A class member that belongs to the class, not an instance; shared by all objects
items.e: static fields and methods belong to the class, not the object. Accessible via the class name without creating an instance.

o: A special method for initializing an object, invoked by new
A method called when the object is destroyed
A method for copying an object
items.e: Constructor: name = class name, no return type. If none is defined, the compiler generates a default (no-arg) one.

o: A reference to the parent class for calling its constructor or methods
A reference to the current object
items.e: super() — calls the parent constructor (as the first statement). super.method() — calls the overridden parent method.

items.q: What are the primitive types in Java?
o: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean
int, long, float, double, String, boolean
byte, int, long, double, char, boolean, String
int, float, double, String, char, boolean, null
items.e: 8 primitive types: byte(1), short(2), int(4), long(8), float(4), double(8), char(2), boolean. String is an object.

items.q: What is the difference between int and Integer?
o: int — a primitive, Integer — a wrapper class supporting null and collections
items.e: int — a primitive type. Integer — a wrapper class with methods. Autoboxing/unboxing converts between them automatically.

o: Automatic conversion of a primitive to its wrapper class
items.e: Autoboxing: int → Integer, double → Double automatically. Unboxing — the reverse. May throw NullPointerException on null.

items.q: What is the default value of an int class field?
items.e: Class fields: int/long/short/byte = 0, float/double = 0.0, boolean = false, char = '\0', Object = null.

o: A heap memory area where String literals are stored for reuse
A list of all program strings
A thread pool for string processing
items.e: String pool (intern pool): "hello" == "hello" → true (one object). new String("hello") == "hello" → false (a new heap object).

items.q: Why is String immutable in Java?
o: Security (passwords, keys), thread safety, String pool optimization
Only because of the String pool
items.e: String immutability: security (a password can't change after being passed), thread-safe, enables the String pool, hashCode is cached.

items.q: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder and StringBuffer?
o: String — immutable; StringBuilder — mutable, not thread-safe; StringBuffer — mutable, thread-safe
String is for numbers, StringBuilder for text
items.e: String is immutable. StringBuilder — mutable, faster (not synchronized). StringBuffer — mutable, thread-safe (synchronized methods).

o: equals() compares string content, == compares references (same object or not)
equals() always returns true for strings
items.e: == compares memory addresses for objects. equals() compares content. For String always use equals().

o: char — the character at position i
items.e: charAt(i) returns the char at position i (0-based). Throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when i is out of range.

o: Splits the string into an array of substrings by a delimiter
items.e: split(regex) returns String[] — an array of substrings. "a,b,c".split(",") → ["a","b","c"].

items.q: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
o: ArrayList — an array (fast get, slow insert/delete in the middle); LinkedList — a doubly-linked list (slow get, fast insert/delete)
ArrayList — linked nodes with fast inserts anywhere; LinkedList — an array with fast random access and less overhead
ArrayList and LinkedList share the same structure, the only difference is synchronization and thread safety
LinkedList is always faster and uses less memory, so ArrayList is almost never used
items.e: ArrayList: O(1) get, O(n) insert/delete in the middle. LinkedList: O(n) get, O(1) insert/delete once you have the node.

items.q: What is the difference between HashMap and TreeMap?
o: HashMap — O(1) get/put, unsorted; TreeMap — O(log n), sorted by key
HashMap is sorted by insertion order
items.e: HashMap: O(1) operations, order not guaranteed. TreeMap: O(log n), keys sorted naturally or via a Comparator.

items.q: What is the difference between HashMap and LinkedHashMap?
o: LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, HashMap doesn't
items.e: LinkedHashMap = HashMap + a doubly-linked list. Preserves insertion order or access order (accessOrder=true).

o: A collection of unique elements with no order, backed by a HashMap
items.e: HashSet is implemented on top of HashMap (element = key, PRESENT = value). Uniqueness via equals() + hashCode().

items.q: What is the equals() and hashCode() contract?
o: If equals() → true, then hashCodes must be equal; but not the other way around
items.e: The contract: equal objects (equals=true) MUST have equal hashCodes. Violations break HashMap and HashSet.

o: An interface for sequential collection traversal with hasNext() and next()
items.e: Iterator: hasNext() checks availability, next() returns the next element, remove() deletes the current one.

o: Thrown when a collection is modified while being iterated
Thrown on concurrent access from different threads
items.e: CME: modifying an ArrayList during for-each throws it. Fixes: Iterator.remove() or CopyOnWriteArrayList.

items.q: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator?
o: Comparable — the class defines its own "natural" order (compareTo); Comparator — an external object for custom sorting
Comparable sets an external order in a service; Comparator always modifies the class and its compareTo()
Comparable works only for numbers and strings; Comparator is only needed for collections with null
Comparable and Comparator play the same role, only the sort method name differs
items.e: Comparable: the class implements compareTo() — one "natural" order. Comparator: a separate object, many different orders.

o: Returns a list wrapper that throws UnsupportedOperationException on modification
items.e: unmodifiableList() — a view that forbids changes. List.of() (Java 9+) — a truly immutable list.

items.q: What is the difference between Queue and Deque?
o: Queue — FIFO from one end; Deque — Double Ended Queue, add/remove from both ends
Queue allows adding from both ends; Deque always works only as a FIFO queue
Deque — a synchronized Queue for multithreading, while Queue is an immutable data structure
Queue and Deque share the same API, only the speed of LinkedList and ArrayDeque differs
items.e: Queue: offer/poll/peek (FIFO). Deque: offerFirst/offerLast/pollFirst/pollLast — can act as both a queue and a stack.

items.q: What is a Stream in Java 8?
o: A sequence of elements supporting a chain of functional operations
items.e: Stream — an abstraction for declarative collection processing: filter, map, reduce. Lazy evaluation, single use.

items.q: What is the difference between intermediate and terminal Stream operations?
o: Intermediate — lazy, return a Stream; terminal — trigger processing, return a result
Intermediate operations run the pipeline immediately and return a collection; terminal ones only add a step
Terminal operations always return a Stream, intermediate ones return a concrete result or void
They are the same, the difference is only whether the method is called before or after filter()
items.e: Intermediate (filter, map, sorted) — lazy, don't run without a terminal. Terminal (collect, forEach, count) — trigger the pipeline.

o: Returns a Stream with the elements matching a predicate
Removes elements from the original collection
items.e: filter(Predicate) keeps only elements where predicate.test() == true. Does not modify the original collection.

o: Transforms every element via a function, returning a new Stream
items.e: map(Function) transforms each element: stream.map(String::toUpperCase) → a Stream of uppercased strings.

o: Turns each element into a Stream and merges all nested Streams into one
items.e: flatMap: List<List<T>> → Stream<T>. Each element becomes a Stream; all are merged into one flat Stream.

o: Collects the Stream elements into a List
items.e: collect() — a terminal operation. Collectors.toList(), toSet(), toMap(), joining(), groupingBy() — popular collectors.

o: Groups elements by a key into a Map<K, List<V>>
items.e: groupingBy(classifier) → Map. stream.collect(groupingBy(Person::getDept)) → Map<String, List<Person>>.

o: Reduces the elements to a single value via a binary operation
items.e: reduce(identity, BinaryOperator): stream.reduce(0, Integer::sum) sums all elements. Returns Optional without an identity.

o: A container that either holds a value or is empty — instead of null
items.e: Optional avoids NullPointerException: Optional.of(), ofNullable(), empty(). Methods: isPresent(), get(), orElse(), map().
distinct() returns a Stream of unique elements. Order is preserved for ordered streams.

items.q: What is the exception hierarchy in Java?
o: Throwable → Error / Exception → RuntimeException / checked exceptions
items.e: Throwable: Error (JVM failures, don't catch) and Exception. Exception: checked (IOException) and unchecked (RuntimeException).

items.q: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
o: Checked — the compiler requires handling (try-catch or throws); unchecked (RuntimeException) — it doesn't
Checked occur only at runtime and aren't compiler-checked; unchecked must always be caught
Unchecked must be declared in throws, while checked can be ignored without try-catch
Checked and unchecked are the same to the compiler, only the log severity differs
items.e: Checked: IOException, SQLException — need try-catch or throws in the signature. Unchecked (RuntimeException): NullPointerException, IndexOutOfBoundsException.

items.q: What does the finally block do?
o: Always runs — on success and on exception — for releasing resources
items.e: finally always runs (except System.exit()). Used for closing resources. Superseded by try-with-resources.

o: try(Resource r = new Resource()) — automatically closes an AutoCloseable resource after the block
items.e: try-with-resources: the compiler automatically calls close() after the block. The class must implement AutoCloseable.

items.q: How do you create a custom exception?
o: Extend Exception or RuntimeException and add constructors
items.e: class MyException extends RuntimeException { MyException(String msg) { super(msg); } } — a simple custom unchecked exception.

o: catch (IOException | SQLException e) — one block for several exception types
items.e: catch (IOException | SQLException e) — concise syntax for identical handling of different exceptions.

o: Parameterized types for type-safe collections and methods without casting
items.e: Generics: List<String> instead of List — type errors are caught at compile time, no explicit cast needed.

items.q: What is the upper bounded wildcard <? extends T>?
o: Accepts T or any subtype of T (covariance) — read-only
Accepts T or any parent type
items.e: <? extends Number> accepts Number, Integer, Double etc. You can read as Number but can't add (Producer Extends).

items.q: What is the lower bounded wildcard <? super T>?
o: Accepts T or any parent type — you can add T (contravariance)
items.e: <? super Integer> accepts Integer, Number, Object. You can add Integer but read only as Object (Consumer Super).

o: Generic types are erased at compilation — at runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are the same
items.e: Type erasure: List<String> → List after compilation. No instanceof List<String> or new T[] at runtime.

items.q: How do you create a thread in Java?
o: Implement Runnable or Callable and pass it to Thread/ExecutorService
items.e: 1) new Thread(runnable).start() 2) ExecutorService.submit(runnable/callable) 3) CompletableFuture. Runnable beats extending Thread.

items.q: What is the difference between Runnable and Callable?
o: Runnable.run() — void, no exceptions; Callable.call() — returns a result and can throw checked exceptions
Runnable.call() returns a Future directly; Callable.run() is only for fire-and-forget tasks
Runnable and Callable are the same, but Callable only works in synchronized ExecutorService blocks
Runnable throws checked exceptions directly; Callable always returns void with no result
items.e: Runnable: void run(). Callable<V>: V call() throws Exception — returns Future<V> when submitted to an ExecutorService.

o: Restricts a method/block to one thread at a time
items.e: A synchronized method or block — only one thread can execute that code at a time. Uses the object's/class's monitor.

o: Guarantees visibility of variable changes across threads — always reads from main memory
items.e: volatile ensures visibility: a change in one thread is immediately visible to others. But no atomicity (doesn't replace synchronized).

o: Two threads hold resources and wait for each other forever
A thread hangs for no reason
items.e: Deadlock: Thread-1 holds A, waits for B; Thread-2 holds B, waits for A — mutual blocking. Fix: always acquire locks in the same order.

o: A thread pool for executing tasks without creating a new Thread each time
items.e: ExecutorService (ThreadPoolExecutor): submit(Callable), execute(Runnable), shutdown(). More efficient than new Thread().

o: The result of an async operation, retrieved via a blocking get() call
items.e: Future<V>: isDone(), cancel(), get() — blocks until the result is available. get(timeout, unit) — with a timeout.

o: A thread-safe Integer for atomic operations without synchronized
items.e: AtomicInteger: incrementAndGet(), compareAndSet() — atomic operations via CAS (Compare-And-Swap) without synchronized blocks.

o: A variable holding a separate value for each thread
items.e: ThreadLocal<T>: each thread has its own value. threadLocal.set(val), threadLocal.get(). Call remove() to avoid memory leaks.

items.q: What are lambda expressions in Java 8?
o: Anonymous functions: (params) -> body — an implementation of a functional interface
items.e: Lambda: (a, b) -> a + b — a short implementation of a @FunctionalInterface. The compiler infers types from context.

o: An interface with exactly one abstract method; default/static methods allowed
An interface with only static methods
items.e: @FunctionalInterface: one abstract method. Standard ones: Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier, BiFunction etc.

o: Shorter syntax for a lambda that just calls an existing method
A reference to a class field
items.e: String::toUpperCase instead of s -> s.toUpperCase(). Kinds: static (Class::method), instance (obj::method), constructor (Class::new).

items.q: What is a default method in an interface (Java 8)?
o: A method with an implementation in the interface — overriding is optional
items.e: default void method() {} in an interface — a default implementation. Lets interfaces evolve without breaking existing classes.

o: An immutable class for a date (year-month-day) without time or time zone
A class for date and time together
A class with a time zone
items.e: LocalDate: now(), of(2024,1,15), plusDays(n), isBefore(). The new Date/Time API (java.time) is safer than Date/Calendar.

o: Parallel element processing in the ForkJoinPool to speed up large datasets
items.e: parallelStream() splits processing across ForkJoinPool threads. Useful for CPU-intensive work on large collections. Not always faster.

items.q: What is the JVM (Java Virtual Machine)?
o: The runtime for Java bytecode — provides platform independence
items.e: The JVM executes .class files (bytecode) on any platform. Includes the ClassLoader, JIT compiler and Garbage Collector.

o: Automatic memory management — frees objects with no references
items.e: The GC automatically finds and removes unreferenced objects. Algorithms: G1, ZGC, Shenandoah, Serial, Parallel.

items.q: What is the difference between Stack and Heap in Java?
o: Stack — method primitives and references (LIFO); Heap — all objects and arrays
Stack — for strings, Heap — for numbers
items.e: Stack: local variables and method parameters, cleaned automatically. Heap: all new objects, managed by the GC.

o: Call stack overflow — usually due to infinite recursion
items.e: StackOverflowError: recursion without an exit condition fills the Stack. It's an Error (not an Exception) — don't catch it.

o: The JVM can't allocate memory for a new object — the heap is full
A memory leak in the Stack
items.e: OOM: "Java heap space" — the heap is full. "GC overhead limit exceeded" — GC takes >98% of time with no effect. Often caused by a memory leak.

items.q: What is a memory leak in Java?
o: Objects that are no longer needed but still referenced — the GC can't remove them
Memory leaks exist only in C/C++
items.e: Memory leaks: static collections that keep growing, unclosed resources, listeners never removed — the GC can't collect referenced objects.

o: Lets an object be used in a for-each loop via its iterator() method
items.e: Iterable<T>: a single iterator() method. Implementing it enables for-each: for (T item : myIterable).

o: An empty interface that tags a class with a certain trait (Serializable, Cloneable)
items.e: Serializable, Cloneable, RandomAccess — marker interfaces with no methods. They signal a capability to the JVM or libraries.

o: A marker interface allowing an object to be serialized into bytes (file, network)
items.e: Serializable: ObjectOutputStream.writeObject() serializes the object. Declaring serialVersionUID explicitly is recommended.

o: Checks whether an object is an instance of a class or implements an interface
items.e: obj instanceof String returns true if obj is a String or a subclass. null instanceof X is always false.

items.q: What is pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16+)?
o: if (obj instanceof String s) — automatically casts the type without an explicit cast
items.e: if (obj instanceof String s) { s.toUpperCase(); } — instead of if (obj instanceof String) { String s = (String) obj; }.

items.q: What is the Predicate<T> functional interface?
o: T -> boolean — a function taking T and returning boolean
items.e: Predicate<T>: test(T t) → boolean. Methods: and(), or(), negate(). Used in Stream.filter().

items.q: What is the Function<T,R> functional interface?
o: T -> R — takes T, returns R
items.e: Function<T,R>: apply(T t) → R. andThen(), compose() for chaining. Used in Stream.map().

items.q: What is the Consumer<T> functional interface?
o: T -> void — takes T, returns nothing (side effect)
items.e: Consumer<T>: accept(T t) → void. Used in Stream.forEach(). andThen() for chaining.

items.q: What is the Supplier<T> functional interface?
o: () -> T — takes no parameters, returns T
items.e: Supplier<T>: get() → T. Handy for lazy initialization: Optional.orElseGet(supplier).

o: Sorts elements naturally or by a Comparator
items.e: sorted() — natural order (Comparable). sorted(Comparator) — custom. A stateful intermediate operation.

o: Returns a Stream with the first n elements
items.e: limit(n) — a short-circuit operation that stops processing after n elements. Useful with infinite Streams.

o: Skips the first n elements and returns the rest
items.e: skip(n) skips the first n elements. Often with limit(n) for pagination: stream.skip(page*size).limit(size).

o: A terminal operation returning the element count as a long
items.e: count() — a terminal operation, returns long. stream.filter(pred).count() — the number of matching elements.

o: Joins the Stream's strings into one string with a delimiter
items.e: Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]") → "[a, b, c]". Joins the Stream's String elements with a delimiter, prefix, suffix.

o: Returns the value for a key, or a default when the key is absent
Adds a default value to the Map
items.e: map.getOrDefault(key, defaultValue) — avoids a null check. map.get(key) returns null when the key is missing.

o: Computes and stores a value for a key only if it's absent
items.e: computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()) — atomically adds a value when the key is missing. Great for Map<K, List<V>>.

items.q: What is a record in Java 16+?
o: An immutable data carrier class with auto-generated equals, hashCode, toString, getters
A regular class with final fields
items.e: record Point(int x, int y) {} — the compiler generates the constructor, x(), y(), equals(), hashCode(), toString(). Immutable.

o: A class that explicitly restricts its subclasses via permits
A class with a private constructor
items.e: sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle {} — only Circle and Rectangle may extend Shape. For ADTs and exhaustive pattern matching.

o: Local type inference — the compiler infers the type from the right-hand side
items.e: var list = new ArrayList<String>() — the compiler infers the type. Local variables only. The code stays statically typed.

o: A switch that returns a value, with -> syntax and no fall-through
items.e: String result = switch(day) { case MONDAY -> "start"; case FRIDAY -> "end"; default -> "mid"; }; — no break, no fall-through.

o: A multi-line string in triple quotes """ without escape characters
items.e: String json = """ { "name": "John" } """; — convenient for JSON, HTML, SQL in tests without extra \n and \.
